title: Capital preservation first: margin of safety and priorities
summary: Before you try to grow wealth, protect the capital you already have, because a large loss takes a much larger gain to repair. A margin of safety is the gap between what you need to be true and what you can prove is true, and it should decide how much you risk.
body:
Bottom line. Protect the capital first and grow it second. A loss of half your money needs a gain of double just to get back to where you started. Build every decision around a margin of safety, which is the room you leave between what you need and what you can prove.

In plain English

Capital is the money and property you already own and could use to make more. Capital preservation means keeping that base intact. It sounds cautious, and it is. It is also simple arithmetic.

Suppose you have 1,000,000 and you lose half. You now have 500,000. To get back to 1,000,000 you must double the 500,000. That is a 100 percent gain to repair a 50 percent loss. Losses and gains are not equal in size, and losses hurt more. A lawyer thinks the same way about risk: some mistakes can be fixed later and some cannot.

A margin of safety is a gap. It is the space between the number you need for a plan to work and the number you can actually prove. If a project works at a sale price of 900,000 and your best evidence says 1,000,000, your margin of safety is 100,000, or 10 percent. If the plan only works at exactly 1,000,000, you have no margin at all. Any surprise lands directly on your capital.

The framework

Use these steps in order. Each one comes before the next for a reason.

  1. Name the capital you cannot afford to lose. This is the money for your home, your family's basic needs, and your tax bills. Write the number down. Call it the protected base.
  2. Separate it from risk capital. Risk capital is money you could lose without changing how your family lives. Only risk capital goes into new ventures.
  3. Find the break-even point of each plan. The break-even point is the result at which you neither gain nor lose. Ask: what price, what cost, what timeline makes this plan stop working?
  4. Measure the margin of safety. Compare the break-even point with the result you can prove with documents. The bigger the gap, the safer the plan.
  5. Set priorities in a fixed order. Survival first, liquidity second, growth third. Liquidity means cash, or something you can turn into cash quickly, without a big discount.
  6. Decide in advance when you will stop. Write a stop rule before you start. For example: if costs rise more than a set amount, pause and review. A rule written in calm conditions is better than a decision made under pressure.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer has 2,000,000 in total capital. He sets 800,000 aside as the protected base: his home equity, a cash reserve for one year of family costs, and money for expected taxes. That leaves 1,200,000 of risk capital.

He is offered a project that needs 1,000,000 of his equity. The project makes money if it sells for more than 4,500,000. His appraiser's written estimate is 5,000,000. The margin of safety is 500,000, which is 10 percent of the estimate.

He tests the margin. If the market falls 10 percent, the sale price drops to 4,500,000 and the project only breaks even. If it falls 15 percent, he loses money. He asks a simple question: can his family absorb losing the full 1,000,000? The answer is yes, because his protected base is untouched. He still decides to commit only 700,000 and to bring in a partner for the rest. That keeps 500,000 of risk capital in reserve for a cost overrun.

The lesson is not that the project is good or bad. The lesson is that the size of the bet now matches the size of the margin.

Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA) or registered financial planner for the household plan; real estate appraiser for the valuation.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to treat the protected base as a source of emergency money for the project. It starts small. A cost overrun arrives, and the developer moves money from the family reserve "just for a month." Then a second overrun arrives. The protected base slowly becomes risk capital without anyone deciding that it should.

The second mistake is to measure the margin of safety against your hopes rather than your proof. A margin built on an assumption is not a margin. It is a second assumption.

How you will use it

Before you sign an offer, a loan, or a personal guarantee, write three numbers on one page: the protected base, the risk capital, and the break-even point of the deal. A personal guarantee is a promise to repay a company's debt from your own money if the company cannot. It reaches straight past your planning and into the protected base, so treat it as part of the bet, not as paperwork.

Use the page in meetings. When your accountant, lender or partner proposes a change, ask which of the three numbers it moves. If it moves the protected base, the answer is no unless you decide, in writing, to change your priorities. This turns a feeling about risk into a decision you can explain and review later.
checklist: Write down the protected base: home, a family cash reserve, and expected taxes.
Calculate risk capital as total capital minus the protected base.
Find the break-even price, cost and timeline for the plan.
Measure the margin of safety against documented evidence, not hopes.
Count any personal guarantee as part of the amount at risk.
Write a stop rule before you commit any money.
Review the page whenever a cost or price assumption changes.

selftest.q: You have 1,500,000 of capital. You set 600,000 aside for your family. A project needs 900,000 of your money and only works if every cost estimate is exactly right. What is your margin of safety, and what should you do?
selftest.a: The margin of safety is zero, because the plan has no room between what must be true and what you can prove. Committing 900,000 would use all of your risk capital and leave nothing for an overrun, so the first surprise would reach the protected base. You should either reduce your commitment, bring in a partner, or require a contingency and a higher proven margin before committing.

apply: On one page, write your protected base, your risk capital, and the break-even point of the next deal you are considering.
sources: Method lesson; no statute, rate or case is cited. All figures are hypothetical and chosen for arithmetic only. The loss-recovery arithmetic (a 50 percent loss needs a 100 percent gain) is basic mathematics. Education only; not financial advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA) or registered financial planner; real estate appraiser for valuations.

title: Asset location vs asset allocation
summary: Asset allocation decides what you own; asset location decides which pocket owns it, such as you personally, your company, a trust or a registered account. The same investment can produce very different after-tax results and very different protection from creditors depending on where it sits.
body:
Bottom line. Allocation is the mix of what you own. Location is which legal pocket holds each piece. Get the mix right first, then put each piece in the pocket where tax, creditor protection and control work best for it.

In plain English

Asset allocation is how you divide your wealth between kinds of assets. For example: some cash, some bonds, some shares in public companies, some real estate, and your own business. Allocation answers the question "what do I own?"

Asset location is a different question. It asks "who owns it, legally?" The same share of a public company can be held by you personally, by your holding company, by a family trust, or inside a registered account such as a Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) or a Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA). These are pockets. Each pocket has its own tax rules, its own exposure to creditors, and its own rules for who controls it and who gets it when you die.

Think of two people with the same mix of assets. One holds everything personally. The other spreads it across pockets with care. They own the same things, but after twenty years they can end up with different results, because the tax and the risk were different all along.

The framework

  1. Set the allocation first. Decide the mix based on your goals, your timeline and your margin of safety. Location never fixes a bad mix.
  2. List your pockets. Personal accounts, registered accounts, an operating company (Opco), a holding company (Holdco), any trust. Write who controls each and who benefits.
  3. Ask four questions for each asset in each pocket. How is its income taxed? Who can reach it if something goes wrong in a business? Who controls it? What happens to it at death?
  4. Match assets to pockets. As a general concept, assets that produce income that is taxed heavily are often better placed in a pocket that shelters or defers that tax. Assets you may need in an emergency should sit where you can reach them without a tax cost or a corporate decision.
  5. Price the cost of moving. Moving an asset from one pocket to another can itself be a sale for tax purposes. Check the cost of the move before you make it.
  6. Write it down as a map. One table: asset, pocket, value, why it sits there, and what would make you move it.

In Canada, registered plans are created under the Income Tax Act (Canada): the RRSP under section 146 and the TFSA under section 146.2. The contribution limits and withdrawal rules change and depend on your own history, so confirm your own room with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) before acting. Corporate investment income is taxed under its own rules, which earlier lessons covered as concepts.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer holds 3,000,000 in total. His chosen allocation is 10 percent cash, 30 percent public market investments, and 60 percent in his business and real estate. That mix stays the same throughout the example.

At first everything outside the business sits in his personal name, including 900,000 of public investments. His Opco carries construction risk and also holds 200,000 of surplus cash it does not need.

His advisers propose a location map. The cash reserve for the family stays personal, because he must reach it quickly. Part of the public investments goes into his registered accounts, up to his available room. The Opco's surplus cash is considered for moving up to the Holdco, away from the Opco's construction creditors, subject to tax advice on how to move it. The real estate stays in separate companies, one per project, so a problem on one site does not reach another.

The allocation did not change at all. Only the pockets changed. The aim is better after-tax growth and fewer assets exposed to a single business failure.

Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA) for tax; corporate lawyer for any transfer between companies.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to move assets between pockets for a tax reason and forget that the move itself can be taxed. Selling an investment to put the cash in another pocket can create a capital gain. Moving property into a company can be a disposition, which means a sale for tax purposes, unless a specific election is properly made.

The second mistake is to let surplus cash pile up inside the company that carries the most risk. Money left in the Opco is money the Opco's creditors can reach.

How you will use it

Draw your location map once a year and after any large event, such as a sale, a new project or a new loan. Bring it to your accountant and ask two questions: "Is anything sitting in the wrong pocket for tax?" and "Is anything sitting in a pocket that carries project risk when it does not need to?" Because you arrive with the map, the meeting is about judgment rather than about collecting facts. That is a shorter and cheaper meeting.
checklist: Fix the allocation (the mix) before thinking about location.
List every pocket: personal, registered accounts, Opco, Holdco, trusts.
For each asset, note tax treatment, creditor exposure, control and what happens at death.
Keep emergency money where you can reach it without tax cost or a corporate decision.
Check whether moving an asset between pockets is itself taxable before moving it.
Do not leave surplus cash in the company that carries the most project risk.
Keep a one-page location map and update it after major events.

selftest.q: Your operating company, which builds projects, has 500,000 of cash it does not need for the next two years. Nothing about your overall investment mix needs to change. What is the location question, and who do you ask?
selftest.a: The allocation is fine; the issue is location. Surplus cash in the Opco is exposed to the Opco's construction creditors. The question is whether to move it to a Holdco or another pocket away from project risk, and how to move it without an unnecessary tax cost. Ask a CPA about the tax treatment of the move and a corporate lawyer to document it properly.

apply: Make a table of your assets with one column for the pocket each sits in and one column for why it sits there.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), section 146 (registered retirement savings plans) and section 146.2 (tax-free savings accounts), cited by name; confirm current text and your personal contribution room with the CRA. Contribution limits and rates are deliberately not stated. All figures hypothetical. Education only; not tax or financial advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA); corporate lawyer for transfers between companies.

title: Liquidity, concentration and the developer's trap
summary: Developers often become wealthy on paper while having little cash, with most of their net worth tied up in a few projects that cannot be sold quickly. That combination of low liquidity and high concentration is the developer's trap, and it is managed by planning cash and spreading risk before you need to.
body:
Bottom line. A developer can be rich on paper and short of cash at the same time. When most of your wealth sits in a few projects that cannot be sold quickly, one bad event can force you to sell at the worst moment. Plan your cash and reduce concentration while things are going well.

In plain English

Liquidity is how fast you can turn an asset into cash without losing much value. Cash in a bank account is fully liquid. A listed share can usually be sold in a day. A half-built project may take a year to sell, and only at a discount.

Concentration means having a large share of your wealth in one asset, one market or one kind of risk. If 80 percent of your net worth is in two buildings in one city, you are highly concentrated.

The developer's trap is the combination of the two. Net worth grows because projects rise in value. But the value is locked in buildings, the buildings carry loans, and the loans often carry personal guarantees. Then something changes: rates rise, a lender asks for more money, a buyer walks away, a partner leaves. The developer needs cash now, and the only way to get it is to sell something illiquid in a hurry. A forced seller rarely gets a good price.

The framework

  1. Count liquid assets separately from net worth. Net worth is assets minus debts. Liquid net worth is only the part you could turn into cash in about a month. Track both.
  2. List every call on your cash. A call on cash is anything that could demand money from you: loan payments, personal guarantees, capital calls from partners, cost overruns, taxes, family needs.
  3. Build a liquidity runway. A runway is how many months you could meet all those calls with liquid assets and no new income. Choose a target and hold to it.
  4. Measure concentration three ways. By single asset, by market or city, and by lender. Three projects with the same bank can be a single risk if that bank changes its policy.
  5. Reduce concentration at good moments. Take some value out when a project succeeds. This can mean refinancing, selling a share, or keeping some profit as cash instead of putting all of it into the next project.
  6. Write down what you would sell first. Decide your order of sale in calm conditions, so you are never choosing it in a crisis.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A developer's statement shows a net worth of 6,000,000. It looks strong. Broken down, 5,400,000 is his equity in three projects in one city, all financed by the same lender. He has 300,000 in cash and 300,000 in listed investments.

His calls on cash: about 25,000 a month of family and office costs, a personal guarantee on a 4,000,000 loan, and a likely capital call of 400,000 next year. His liquid assets of 600,000 cover the capital call and about eight months of costs, but nothing more.

Now a test. The lender reviews the loan and asks for 500,000 to bring it back within its loan-to-value limit, which is the maximum loan allowed as a share of the property's value. He has 600,000 of liquidity. After paying it, only 100,000 is left, and the capital call is still coming. He must either sell a project quickly or borrow on worse terms.

His plan in response: when the first project completes, he keeps 1,000,000 of the profit as cash rather than putting all of it into a fourth project. He also uses a second lender for the next project. His net worth barely changes. His exposure to one bad letter from one bank falls sharply.

Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA) for cash-flow planning; lawyer for any guarantee or loan amendment.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to treat a strong net worth as proof of safety. Lenders, partners and markets do not ask what you are worth. They ask whether you can pay on the due date.

The second mistake is reinvesting every profit straight into the next project because the last one went well. Success increases concentration unless you deliberately take some value out. A third mistake is to forget that personal guarantees are calls on your cash even when nothing has gone wrong yet. They do not appear on a simple list of debts, but a lender can call on them quickly.

How you will use it

Keep a one-page liquidity sheet, separate from your balance sheet. It shows liquid assets, every call on your cash, and your runway in months. Update it each quarter and before signing any guarantee. When you review a new deal, ask how it changes three things: your runway, your share of wealth in one city, and your share of debt with one lender. If a deal shortens the runway below your target, it needs a reason strong enough to write down.
checklist: Track liquid net worth separately from total net worth.
List every call on your cash, including personal guarantees and capital calls.
Calculate your runway in months and set a minimum target.
Measure concentration by asset, by city, and by lender.
Keep part of each project's profit as cash instead of reinvesting all of it.
Decide your order of sale before you are under pressure.
Recheck the runway before signing any new guarantee or loan.

selftest.q: Your net worth is 5,000,000, but 4,500,000 is in two projects with the same bank and you have 200,000 in cash. A third project is offered that needs 300,000 of your equity and another personal guarantee with the same bank. What does the developer's trap framework tell you?
selftest.a: Taking the deal would leave you with no liquid runway, raise your concentration with one lender, and add another call on your cash through the guarantee. The framework says to first rebuild liquidity, for example by keeping profit from a completed project or bringing in a partner, and to use a different lender if you proceed. A strong paper net worth does not change the fact that you could not meet a demand for cash.

apply: Calculate your liquid net worth and your runway in months, and write both at the top of your balance sheet.
sources: Method lesson; no statute, rate or case is cited. Loan-to-value is defined conceptually; actual lender limits vary by lender and loan. All figures hypothetical. Education only; not financial advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: chartered professional accountant (CPA); lawyer for guarantees and loan amendments.

title: Generational design: control today, transfer tomorrow
summary: Good generational design separates control from value, so you can keep making decisions today while future growth passes to the next generation. It also plans for people, because a family business needs heirs who can carry it and a founder whose identity does not depend on holding every role.
body:
Bottom line. You can keep control of your business while moving its future growth to your children. The tools separate who decides from who benefits. The harder part is human: heirs need preparation, and you need an identity that is bigger than the job you do today.

In plain English

Most founders want two things that seem to conflict. They want to keep running the business. They also want wealth to pass to the next generation without a large tax bill or a family fight.

The answer is to separate control from value. Control means the right to make decisions, usually through voting shares or a role as director or trustee. Value means the right to the money, through growth, dividends or proceeds of a sale. Corporate and trust tools let these sit with different people.

A common Canadian concept is the estate freeze. In an estate freeze, the founder exchanges his common shares for fixed-value preferred shares. Preferred shares are shares with a fixed value and set rights. New common shares are then issued, often to the children or to a family trust, for a small amount. All future growth goes to the new common shares. The founder's value is frozen at today's amount, which limits the tax at his death to today's gain. He can keep control through voting rights. These exchanges are commonly done under section 86 or section 85 of the Income Tax Act (Canada). The details are technical and must be designed by professionals.

The framework

  1. Write the goal in one sentence. For example: "I keep control for ten years; growth goes to my children; my spouse is secure."
  2. Separate control and value on paper. Who should vote? Who should benefit? They do not need to be the same people.
  3. Choose the tool. A freeze, a family trust, a holding company, or a shareholder agreement. Each was covered in earlier lessons as a concept.
  4. Plan the handover of control in stages. Decide what the next generation earns the right to decide, and when. Put milestones in writing.
  5. Prepare the people. Heirs need financial education, a role and a voice before they inherit power.
  6. Plan for the founder's next role. Decide what you will do, and who you will be, after you step back.
  7. Review every few years. Laws, family and business all change.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. All numbers are round and invented for teaching.

A founder's company is worth 4,000,000. He has two adult children. He exchanges his common shares for preferred shares worth 4,000,000 and keeps voting control. A family trust subscribes for new common shares for 100. The trust's beneficiaries are his children, and he and his spouse are trustees.

Ten years later the company is worth 10,000,000. His preferred shares are still worth 4,000,000. The 6,000,000 of growth belongs to the common shares in the trust. At his death, the tax on his shares is measured against the frozen 4,000,000, not against 10,000,000. Meanwhile he has kept the vote throughout.

One warning: a family trust in Canada is generally treated as disposing of its property every 21 years under section 104(4) of the Income Tax Act (Canada). The trust's plan must account for that date.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax lawyer and chartered professional accountant (CPA) for the freeze and the trust; business valuator for the fair market value.

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is to treat generational design as a tax exercise only. The structure works and the family does not. Children who never learned the business inherit control they cannot use. Or the founder keeps every decision until the last day, so nobody is ready.

There is a quieter mistake: the founder's whole sense of self is the business. Then stepping back feels like loss, so it never happens. This connects to a point from the course's source episode. In a podcast interview, Greg Baker, a computing lecturer at Macquarie University, described representing himself at Australia's Fair Work Commission with the help of AI tools. As reported, he won (Baker v Macquarie University [2026] FWC 3054). Baker says a profession is not a person, and that people should build an identity beyond their role, because roles change. That is his opinion, not settled fact. But it applies to founders too. A founder who knows who he is outside the business can hand it over.

How you will use it

Write two short documents. The first is a control map: who votes, who benefits, who replaces whom, and when. The second is a personal note on what you will do after you step back from daily decisions. Bring the first to your tax lawyer and accountant before any freeze or trust is set up. Share the second with your family, so the handover is a plan everyone understands rather than a surprise. Review both every three to five years.
checklist: Write your generational goal in one sentence.
List separately who should control and who should benefit.
Get a professional valuation before any estate freeze.
Note the 21-year date for any family trust.
Set written milestones for handing over decisions.
Give heirs financial education and a real role before they inherit control.
Write down what your role and identity will be after you step back.

selftest.q: A founder wants his children to receive the future growth of his company but is not ready to let them make decisions. His accountant suggests giving them half his voting shares now. What is the better design question?
selftest.a: The design should separate control from value. Giving voting shares transfers both control and value at once, which he does not want. A freeze can move future growth to the children or a family trust through new common shares while he keeps voting control through his preferred shares or as trustee. He should then plan staged handover of control and prepare the children. A tax lawyer, CPA and valuator must sign off.

apply: Draw a two-column table: who decides today, and who benefits from growth, for each company and trust you own.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 85 (transfer of property to a corporation), section 86 (exchange of shares in a reorganization) and section 104(4) (21-year deemed disposition for trusts), cited by name; confirm current text before relying on them. Source episode: Greg Baker on the At The Top podcast (https://youtu.be/mrBWJYkDNkI); decision Baker v Macquarie University [2026] FWC 3054, 12 August 2026, as reported by Monash Lens, Lawyers Weekly, ACS Information Age and The Lawyer Mag. Baker's views are his opinions; read the decision before quoting it. Figures hypothetical. Education only.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax lawyer and chartered professional accountant (CPA); business valuator.
